evals.prompt: Define a React ref in 2-3 sentences. Explain its shape and how it relates to the render cycle.
expected_elements: A ref is a mutable object `{ current: T }` created by useRef(initial) that persists across renders
Writing to ref.current does NOT trigger a re-render; reading does NOT subscribe the component to changes
The ref lives outside the reactive graph / outside the render cycle
Names the two canonical uses: DOM access and mutable instance values

evals.prompt: Why does a ref persist across renders without participating in the render cycle, and what two families of values is it the right primitive for?
expected_elements: React creates the { current } container once per component instance and returns the same object every render
Family 1: DOM access — a stable handle to a DOM node for focus, measurement, animation, or non-React library handoff
Family 2: mutable instance values — interval id, rAF id, latest-args closure, previous-value snapshot that drive side effects but are not rendered
The ref exists outside the reactive graph, which is why it does not cause or subscribe to re-renders

evals.prompt: An engineer wants to store a frequently-changing value and says 'I'll use a ref instead of state to avoid re-renders.' Explain the real trade-off and how to decide.
expected_elements: The choice is SEMANTIC, not a performance optimization: ref = outside the render cycle, state = inside it
The sharp rule: if the value should cause a re-render when it changes, it is state; if not, it is a ref — no middle ground
Using a ref to dodge re-renders for a value the UI must reflect breaks the contract: the value changes but the UI does not update
useMemo (not a ref) is the answer for caching an expensive value derived from inputs

evals.prompt: A parent needs to open and close a child Modal imperatively. Apply this skill to design the API, and state the discipline rules.
expected_elements: Expose a controlled handle via useImperativeHandle (e.g. { open, close }) attached to the forwarded ref, not the raw DOM node
Expose the MINIMUM surface the parent needs — the parent's ref is a public API
Do not expose state-read functions; if the parent must read state, lift it up
Default to props: most cases are better as an isOpen prop + onOpenChange callback than an imperative handle

evals.prompt: A consumer attaches a ref to a compound-component primitive (e.g. <Tabs.Trigger ref={...}>) to focus it on mount, but ref.current stays null. Apply this skill to diagnose and fix it.
expected_elements: Every layer between the consumer and the underlying DOM element must forward the ref
The fix is to forward refs through each primitive part to its DOM node (Radix Slot / composeRefs pattern merges consumer + internal refs)
Diagnose by checking that intermediate wrappers accept and pass the ref rather than dropping it
A compound-component library that does not forward refs through every primitive is not finished

evals.prompt: A teammate asks the ref-patterns skill to decide whether the app's form state should live in the URL, on the server, or in client state, and to set the dependency-array rules for the project's effects. Is that in scope? Why or why not?
expected_elements: State location/ownership (server / client UI / URL / persistent) is state-management's territory, not ref-patterns
Dependency-array discipline, Rules of Hooks, and effect rules belong to hooks-patterns
ref-patterns owns the not-state mutable-handle primitive and the ref-vs-state decision boundary, plus the ref family (useRef, forwardRef, useImperativeHandle, ref callbacks)
Correctly redirects rather than over-owning state architecture or hook discipline

evals.prompt: Someone says 'refs and state are just two mutable-value options — use a ref if you don't want a re-render, state if you do.' Correct the mental model.
expected_elements: The sentence is true but incomplete — it frames a semantic distinction as a performance optimization
Refs are for values OUTSIDE the render cycle (drive side effects, not displayed); state is for values INSIDE it (changing them must re-evaluate the output)
Names concrete failures: useRef holding form values that should be useState (UI does not update on edit); useState holding interval ids that should be useRef (re-render storm per tick)
Do not present 'no re-render' as a free optimization knob

evals.prompt: What would you check when reviewing a component's ref usage to verify it follows this skill?
expected_elements: Every ref is a DOM ref or a mutable instance value — never a substitute for state that drives the UI
ref.current is read only inside effects, event handlers, or callbacks — never during render; no DOM nodes in useState
Compound-component primitives forward refs; useImperativeHandle exposes the minimum surface (props + callbacks considered first)
No ref is passed across the 'use client' boundary as a prop from a Server Component; ref-held resources have cleanup paths
On React 19, new code uses ref-as-prop; existing forwardRef retained for back-compat or codemod-migrated

evals.prompt: A Server Component renders a child and wants to pass it a ref to measure it on the server. Apply this skill to explain what happens and what to do instead.
expected_elements: Refs only work in Client Components; a ref cannot be created in a Server Component, passed across the 'use client' boundary, or returned from a Server Action (not serializable)
Server Components produce HTML on the server — there is no DOM node and no client runtime to hold the mutable container
Move the part of the tree that needs the ref into a Client Component marked 'use client'
The broader boundary mechanics belong to client-server-boundary; this is the ref-specific consequence
